documentation.range: The current distribution of Tomistoma schlegelii extends over lowland regions of eastern Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sarawak and Peninsular Malaysia (Malaysia) (Stuebing et al. 2006). The presence of the species in western Java is questionable. Historically, T. schlegelii apparently occurred in southern Thailand, but there have been no reports of the species there since at least the 1970s and it is probably now extirpated from there (Ratanakorn et al. 1994, Stuebing et al. 2006). There are unconfirmed reports from Sabah (Borneo), Sulawesi (Indonesia) and Viet Nam, but these are not substantiated, and the lack of documented records suggests the species did not occur in these locations or that historic populations no longer remain there (Stuebing et al. 2006).
documentation.population:
Tomistoma schlegelii is a cryptic species and its swamp forest habitats are difficult to access: many surveys may have under-recorded or not detected its presence. Compared with spotlight densities for some other crocodilians, which may reach densities of tens or hundreds of individuals per kilometre, recorded densities of T. schlegelii remain low. In accessible survey areas, standardised eyeshine surveys have allowed for accurate estimation of the relative abundance of T. schlegelii. In a 2018 project within Sarawak, wild T. schlegelii were recorded using inexpensive infrared CCTV cameras, capable of detecting eyeshine at a distance >75 metres  (A. Pine, unpub. data). Few other methods to estimate abundance have been applied to T. schlegelii. A mark-recapture study was conducted from 2010–2011 at Mesangat Lake (East Kalimantan Province, Indonesia) but few individuals have been recaptured (Staniewicz 2012). Nest census methods have not been applied to T. schlegelii because nests are located in swamp forest and are highly cryptic.

The largest extant populations of T. schlegelii are in Indonesia (Sumatra and Kalimantan) and Malaysia (Sarawak). In Sumatra, the species was widely distributed prior to the 1950s in the lowlands of the eastern portion of the island, but intensive hunting from the 1950s to 1970s and habitat loss had reduced this range by around 30% by the late 1990s (Bezuijen et al. 1998). Scattered populations persist from North Sumatra to South Sumatran provinces, with an isolated population in Way Kambas National Park. Tomistoma schlegelii is not reported west of the Barisan Mountain Ranges (Bezuijen et al. 1998). Spotlight surveys generally produce extremely low observed densities. However Shaney et al. (2016, 2019) recently recorded an unusually high density (1.38 individuals/km) in the Simpang T, a tributary of the Air Hitam Luat River in Jambi Province. Pine (unpub. data) recorded one of the highest densities (mean density of 2.21 ± 0.58 individuals/km) in an isolated river system within the Sebuyau sub-district of Sarawak. Typically, maximum spotlight densities may reach 0.18 or 0.26 individuals/km as recorded in South Sumatra and Jambi Provinces respectively (Bezuijen et al. 2002a).

In Kalimantan, documented breeding populations persist in the Mesangat wetlands (Stuebing et al. 2015) and Mahakam River in East Kalimantan Province (Meijard and Sozer 1996, Ross et al. 1998), Tanjung Puting National Park in Central Kalimantan Province (Simpson 2004, Auliya et al. 2006), and Danau Sentarum and Gunung Palung National Parks (pers. comm. to A. Pine, 2022), and the upper Kapaus River in West Kalimantan Province (Bezuijen et al. 2004, Simpson and Mediyansyah 2009). There are no confirmed wild populations in South Kalimantan Province. A small breeding population, along a well-protected short (<4 km) river section near the headquarters of Tanjung Puting National Park, is the most secure T. schlegelii population globally, and the park also supports the highest documented densities of this species (1.4 individuals/km) (Simpson 2004, Auliya et al. 2006). It is notable that in areas of the park further from the headquarters, habitats are more disturbed and T. schlegelii densities are much lower (Auliya et al. 2006). In Danau Sentarum National Park (West Kalimantan Province), spotlight densities at a site ranged from 0.21 individuals/km in 1994 (Frazier 1994) to 0.08 individuals/km in 2004 (Bezuijen et al. 2004), and 0.02–0.07 individuals/km at other sites (Bezuijen et al. 2004, Simpson and Mediyansyah 2009). At Mesangat Lake (East Kalimantan Province), T. schlegelii is locally abundant. In 2012, densities ranged from 0.2–1.6 individuals/km in flooded forest and open water habitats (Staniewicz 2012).

In Malaysia, small breeding populations were reported from Sarawak (local reports from Kuching, Bintulu and Miri Divisions in western, central and northwestern Sarawak) (Bezuijen et al. 2010). Recent fieldwork has documented additional breeding populations occurring in the Sebuyau sub-district (A. Pine, unpub. obs.). In Peninsular Malaysia, a breeding population was documented from the Sitiu wetlands, Terengganu in 2008 (S. Anwar pers. comm. 2014), while T. schlegelii were present in the Perak River in 2004. Tomistoma schlegelii are occasionally reported from the North Selangor peat swamp forest, Pahang Rivers and Tesak Bera Ramsar site (Stuebing et al. 2004, 2006; Simpson 2014). Remnant populations still remain in Peninsular Malaysia yet are small, fragmented and severely threatened, especially given the extensive and continuing loss of natural wetland habitats and high human densities of this region.

In Brunei, the first documented evidence of T. schlegelii was obtained in 2005, with an individual being photographed in the Sungai Tutong River (R. Stuebing, pers. comm. 2010). There is no reason to suggest this was a released individual and it is the first confirmed national record. However, few crocodile surveys have been conducted to date (e.g. Das and Charles 2000, Cox 2006) and possibly none targeting inland swamp forests, where T. schlegelii are most likely to occur.

Although these data suggest a wide current distribution, it is likely that most remnant breeding populations of T. schlegelii are highly threatened and under continuing pressure (see the Threats section).

A wild crocodile captured in 1967 in Viet Nam was reported to be this species (Mucelli 2005). Given the severe threats facing two confirmed crocodile species in Viet Nam, Crocodylus siamensis and C. porosus, it seems likely that even if T. schlegelii was present historically, it has now been extirpated. Similarly in Thailand, T. schlegelii were reported to have occurred (e.g. Smith 1916, Taylor 1970) but records are vague and inconclusive. Given that no further reports have been made since at least the 1970s, previous authors have postulated the species may be extirpated (Humphrey and Bain 1990, Ratanakorn 1994) or that historical records may have referred to localities in northern Peninsular Malaysia (Stuebing et al. 2006).

Tomistoma schlegelii is legally protected in all Range States, and occurs in several national parks, but the level of applied protection is insufficient to protect breeding habitats.

Captive T. schlegelii are held in private facilities and zoos in Asia, Europe and North America and probably number a few thousand individuals in total. The largest captive population is at Utairatch Crocodile Farm in Thailand (over 700 individuals). Successful breeding has occurred at Jong’s Crocodile Farm and Zoo (Sarawak), Samutprakan, Utairatch and Pattaya Crocodile Farms (Thailand) and in zoos in Malaysia, Europe and North America. Tomistoma schlegelii has no commercial skin value, precluding conservation efforts based on ranching as conducted for some other crocodilian species.
documentation.habitats:
Tomistoma is a freshwater, mound-nesting crocodilian with a distinctively long, narrow snout. It is one of the largest of the extant crocodilians, with males attaining lengths of up to 5 m (Bezuijen et al. 1998, 2004). It is restricted primarily to lowland swamps, lakes and rivers. Most records are from peat swamp and freshwater swamp forest (Stuebing et al. 2006), which historically encompassed most of the lowlands of Borneo, eastern Sumatra, and Peninsular Malaysia.

Few data are available on nesting ecology and less than 20 wild nests have been documented. Four nests in eastern Sumatra were located in mature peat swamp forest in remote upstream tributaries and were situated at the base of large trees (Bezuijen et al. 1998, 2001b, 2002a). Three nests in Sarawak have been reported, with one in degraded forest at the edge of cultivated land (Lading and Stuebing 1997), one along an isolated swamp forest tributary within an elevated brush mound (A. Pine, unpub. obs.), and another within a flooded swamp forest adjacent to a village (A. Pine, unpub. obs.). In Kalimantan, nests have been recorded on floating vegetation mats (Ross et al. 1998). Nesting occurs in the dry season and Tomistoma lays small clutches (13–41 eggs per nest; Endert 1927, Bezuijen et al. 2001b). The eggs are the largest eggs of the extant crocodilians (Bezuijen et al. 1998, 2001b). Sexual maturity in females appears to be attained at around 2.5–3 m total length and 20 years age (Bezuijen et al. 1998; Shwedick 2006; Brazaitis and Abene 2008; B. Ziegler [Miami Metro Zoo, USA] pers. comm., 1995; U. Youngprapakorn [Utairatch Crocodile Farm & Zoo, Thailand]) pers. comm., 2008), a relatively large size and late age compared with other crocodilians. Hatchlings emerge in the late dry season / early wet season after an estimated 70–80 days incubation (Bezuijen et al. 1997).

Müller (1838) stated the diet of T. schlegelii comprised fish, monitor lizards (Varanus), waterbirds and mammals. Predation of monkeys by T. schlegelii has been observed (Galdikas and Yeager 1984, Galdikas 1985, Yeager 1991). Stomach contents of juvenile wild T. schleglii included shrimp (Bezuijen et al. 1998) and other invertebrates (Staniewicz and Behler 2010).

Despite being generally regarded as harmless to humans, there have been a number of incidents of predation on humans by Tomistoma (Rachmawan and Brend 2009), and one confirmed case of a cow being attacked in a wetland habitat in East Kalimantan (R. Stueubing, pers. comm. 2010). Since 2010, 30 incidents have been recorded in the Worldwide Crocodilian Attack Database (CrocBITE 2013). Of these, 10 were fatal.

Other scientific studies of T. schlegelii have included assessment of its taxonomic status (see the Taxonomic Notes section), anatomy and skin qualities (e.g. Boulenger 1896, King and Brazaitis 1971, Brazaitis 1973, Fuchs 2006), potential impacts of climate change (Bickford et al. 2010), conservation effectiveness of protected area networks (Rödder et al. 2010), and captive breeding and management (see the Conservation Measures section).
documentation.threats:
Severe and continuing loss of swamp forest habitat throughout the global range of T. schlegelii is the key threat to most wild populations. Loss and fragmentation of swamp forest has been occurring for over four decades throughout Southeast Asia due to large-scale commercial and illegal logging, plantation development (especially the establishment of paper pulp mills and palm oil plantations), forest fires, and deliberate swamp drainage through construction of channels and dykes. Large areas of swamp forest in East, Central and West Kalimantan were destroyed or severely degraded by the El Niño-induced drought of 1997 and 1998 (Stibig et al. 2007). The expansion of oil palm plantations is currently the main driver of loss of swamp forest in Sumatra and Borneo (Stibig et al. 2007). Based on satellite imagery from 2000, almost 45% (more than one million hectares) of peat swamp in Peninsular Malaysia and Thailand has been converted to various land uses, and over a million hectares has been converted in Borneo and Sumatra (Yoshino et al. 2010). Across the global range of T. schlegelii, Borneo retains the largest area of peat swamp under natural cover (70–90%), but which is of varying quality and much is degraded (Yoshino et al. 2010).

In Sarawak, a potential and localised threat to the distribution of T. schlegelii is in the range overlap of Crocodylus porosus. Although this threat is still poorly understood, in areas where C. porosus are overly abundant, T. schlegelii appears to retreat into areas that may offer less favourable conditions and resources.

At least in Sumatra, a significant threat appears to be predation of T. schlegelii eggs by the introduced Wild Pig, Sus scrofa. Four of seven T. schlegelii nests recorded along one river were predated by Wild Pigs (Bezuijen et al. 1997). A smaller, but potentially significant, threat is opportunistic removal of individuals and eggs from the wild, usually by residents and crocodile farmers (see the Use and Trade section). Commercial hunting of T. schlegelii occurred in some regions from the 1950s–1970s and probably contributed to the decline of the species, but this no longer occurs. Individuals sometimes drown in fishing nets. In areas with depressed and threatened populations, the continuing low-level removal of mature individuals (e.g. from drowning or capture in fishing gear) may cause disproportionately large impacts. This may be the case along some rivers in southern Sumatra (Bezuijen et al. 2001a). Accidental mortality of T. schlegelii have occurred during river excavation and dredging activities within Sarawak (A. Pine, pers. obs.).

Targeted fishing of T. schelgelii appears to be a minor threat in East Kalimantan (Indonesia) and Sarawak (Malaysia), where fishermen often release T. schlegelii caught in fishing gear due to local beliefs that harming the species will bring bad luck or illness (RBS, pers. obs.; Pine, pers. obs.). The impact of fishing activities on prey and habitat availability, and the potential competition between fishermen and T. schlegelii, is poorly understood.
documentation.measures:
High Priority

1. Initiate conservation programs at key sites in Sarawak, Sumatra and Kalimantan: Although large information gaps remain in our knowledge of the distribution and ecology of T. schlegelii, there is now sufficient information to develop well-planned field conservation programs at some sites. Extended funding is required to develop and implement such programs to secure documented breeding populations of T. schlegelii in Indonesia. The highest priority sites for conservation are:

a. Sebuyau sub-district, Sarawak. Surveys in 2016–2018, initiated by Universiti Malaysia Sarawak (UNIMAS), identified an accessible breeding population of T. schlegelii in the Sebuyau sub-district (A. Pine, unpub. obs.).

b. Danau Sentarum (DSNP) and Gunung Palung National Parks, West Kalimantan. DSNP and the neighbouring Kapuas river system provide opportunities to survey T. schlegelii, with the best likelihood occurring during the dry season when the species is most likely to be observed (A. Pine, pers. obs.). DSNP has ongoing governmental surveys of T. schlegelii being led by local forestry officials offering opportunities for sustainable collaboration.

c. Tanjung Puting National Park (TPNP), Central Kalimantan; Based on the information obtained during a CSG-TTF site visit to TPNP in 2014, an opportunity does exist to upgrade the use of T. schlegelii as an iconic species, and to implement various programs that provide ongoing monitoring indices of the population over time. This program should be developed and managed by TPNP and include participation from the park’s freelance guides and NGOs which operate within park borders. With relatively minor changes, increased reporting associated with current activities could provide useful data to assess population trends, document movements, gain further information on the absolute size and structure of the population, and add significantly to our knowledge of natural history and ecology.

d. A project has been initiated in Danau Mesangat by the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS Indonesia) in collaboration with the CSG-TTF. Further surveys will be necessary to determine the status of T. schlegelii in other areas of East Kalimantan.

e. Merang River, Berbak National Park and Way Kambas National Park, Sumatra.

2. Clarify the status of T. schlegelii and strengthen national coordination for T. schlegelii conservation in Sarawak. Work with national agencies to identify and assess the distribution and status of T. schlegelii in Sarawak, including previously reported breeding sites. Implement and promote the conservation of T. schlegelii populations.

Moderate Priority

3. Clarify the status of T. schlegelii in other locations in Sumatra and Kalimantan. The distribution and status of T. schlegelii over much of Sumatra and Kalimantan remains poorly documented. Rapid assessments are required to identify new breeding populations where local reports suggest that T. schlegelii may still occur, particularly at the following sites: Jambi, Riau and North Sumatra Provinces in Sumatra; Muara Kendawangan Nature Reserve in West Kalimantan; and, Lamandau Wildlife Reserve in Central Kalimantan.

4. Quantify status of T. schlegelii in Peninsular Malaysia. Identifying and confirming T. schlegelii sites will first be required in Peninsular Malaysia before further actions can be implemented. It is evident that if T. schlegelii initiatives are to be successful in the North Selangor peat swamp forest, the Tengi River would provide the best site for population protection/recovery. This site is in relatively good condition and well protected, surrounded by the Raja Musa and Sungai Kerang Forestry Reserves, and the Sungai Dusun Wildlife Reserve. The remaining T. schlegelii population there would also benefit from population augmentation, with the introduction of additional animals. The modification of the swamp forest may also be required to provide wetlands more suitable for T. schlegelii. This could include the blocking and expanding (width and depth) of existing drainage canals, and the provisions of small ponds (dry season refuges) within the peat swamp forest itself. Fishing regulations may also be warranted. Surveys are required to clarify status and identify conservation priorities at: Setiu wetlands and Sungai Tengi (Terangganu State), Jelud River and other wetlands near the Thai border, eastern Pahang, including the Pahang River and Lake Chini, and the upper Perak River.

Lower Priority

5. Increase production and dissemination of educational materials for promoting interest, awareness, research, and conservation of T. schlegelii. There is a significant lack of awareness efforts and relevant materials in areas with wild populations of T. schlegelii. As the protection of habitat within these areas are often community-driven, resources should be allocated towards bolstering localised interest, efforts and partnerships.

6. Quantify the status of T. schlegelii in Brunei, Sabah (Malaysia) and western Java (Indonesia). The presence of T. schlegelii in Java and Brunei has recently been reported (Stuebing et al. 2006). Examination of available records, including museum specimens, and site visits could shed light on the status of the species at these locations.



Conservation Initiatives

In 2003 the CSG Tomistoma Task Force (CSG-TTF) was formed. Current conservation initiatives led by the CSG-TTF include fundraising for field research (e.g. the first detailed autecological study of T. schlegelii by Rene Bonke in Central Kalimantan), providing voluntary technical support through its members to Range States, and raising international awareness of T. schlegelii. A CSG-TTF website and web-based user group was created in 2003 to encourage public participation and since then several fund-raising events led by Bruce Shwedick, Ralf Sommerlad and other members have been held in North America and Europe. CSG-TTF reports have been prepared on T. schlegelii conservation priorities (Bezuijen et al. 2003) and standards for captive breeding (Shwedick and Sommerlad 2000, Shwedick 2004). In 2004, the CSG-TTF, along with the People Resources and Conservation Foundation (PRCF) and National Geographic Television, provided funding for surveys of T. schlegelii in DSNP and other areas in West Kalimantan. In 2005, a short-term assessment of T. schlegelii was conducted by Mark Auliya and Stephen Brend in Tanjung Puting National Park and this was followed by a 2008 population ecology study led by Rene Bonke. An international CSG-TTF workshop was held in 2008 and resulted in an updated list of global conservation priorities.

In East Kalimantan Province, a new conservation foundation, Yayasan Ulin, was founded in 2009 to promote local T. schlegelii conservation in the Mesangat wetlands. Field studies of T. schlegelii at Mesangat were subsequently conducted in 2009–2012 (Staniewicz 2013, Stuebing et al. 2015). In 2010 PRCF began planning T. schlegelii conservation activities in DSNP and surrounding areas. In 2013, the project “Focused Conservation of Tomistoma schlegelii in the Landscape of Danau Sentarum National Park, West Kalimantan, Indonesia” was established between DSNP and PRCF. The first phase of this project (Suriansyah et al. 2017) was funded by the CSG-TTF and PRCF.

Recent status assessment surveys in Peninsular Malaysia and in Sumatra have also been supported by the CSG-TTF. In November 2017, a training workshop on crocodilian veterinary medicine and conservation was organized by BKSDA Aceh and the Center for Wildlife Studies at the Veterinary Faculty of the Syiah Kuala University Banda Aceh, a was held in Medan, Indonesia, with a program developed by the CSG’s Veterinary Science Working Group and CSG-TTF. Representatives from five regional field offices of the Indonesian Ministry of Forests, as well as veterinarians and wildlife rescue workers participated in the workshop’s intensive four-day program (Stevenson 2017). A second professional training course and workshop on medical management, conflict management and conservation of crocodiles, with a special focus on Crocodylus porosus and Tomistoma schlegelii, was held in Balikpapan, Indonesia on 15–18 November 2019 (Stevenson 2020). Both workshops also provided opportunities for field site visits along with an initiative to encourage Indonesian university students to undertake field research focusing on T. schlegelii and its habitats (Shwedick and Wasilewski 2020, Shwedick et al. 2020).

In 2012, a children’s book about T. schlegelii was written and printed for conservation efforts by Anthony Pine of The Tomistoma Fund (defunct). Written in Bahasa Melayu and English, this book was published in 2016 and distributed during research and conservation programs throughout Sarawak and parts of West Kalimantan. There is a need to further promote conservation and awareness of T. schlegelii to the public and to children in areas where the species persists.

Despite these positive efforts, T. schlegelii conservation is hindered by a lack of large and sustained funding. All projects have been conducted with minor funding and by virtue of their brief duration have been insufficient to develop expanded conservation programs. This is also due to the fact that most personnel working on the species have done so almost entirely on a voluntary basis. There is a realistic need to assign, and properly fund full-time persons who will coordinate T. schlegelii conservation, prepare large funding proposals, and initiate projects with local agencies.

Tomistoma schlegelii has no commercial skin value, precluding conservation efforts based on ranching as conducted for some other crocodilians.
documentation.use_trade:
Small-scale opportunistic collection of wild individuals and eggs occurs in some regions, for sale to crocodile farms and/or consumption. The species was previously hunted in some regions for skins and/or meat.

Tomistoma schlegelii is listed under Appendix I of CITES. Captive individuals are held in zoos and private facilities (mainly crocodile farms) around the world, and probably number a few thousand individuals in total. The largest captive population (700+) is at Utairatch Crocodile Farm in Thailand. Successful breeding has occurred at Jong's Crocodile Farm (Sarawak), Utairatch and Pattaya Crocodile Farms (Thailand), and irregularly at zoos in Malaysia, Europe and North America although optimisation to husbandry procedures are seeing an improvement in captive reproduction (Litton et al. 2018). The provenance of most captive individuals is unclear leaving many wild-caught T. schlegelii held in captivity of limited value for conservation purposes unless their original provenance can be determined.

Residents in Sumatra, West Kalimantan and Peninsular Malaysia report that T. schlegelii, as well as other crocodilians, were hunted in the 1950s–1970s for the commercial skin trade, and their meat and eggs were sometimes collected (Bezuijen et al. 1998, 2004; Simpson et al. 1998; Simpson and Mediyansyah 2009). In contrast, hunters in East Kalimantan and Sarawak state the species has no commercial value and was not hunted. Commercial skin trade no longer occurs. Tomistoma schlegelii is not a commercially valuable species due to the presence of osteoderms in the belly scales (Fuchs 2006). Low-level but ongoing removal of T. schlegelii from the wild continues. In Sumatra, wild juvenile T. schlegelii at a crocodile farm in 2002 had been purchased from local fishermen, and staff reported that the farm continues to purchase T. schlegelii on an opportunistic basis. In 1997, juvenile T. schlegelii observed at the facility of a wildlife trader on Penang Island, Peninsular Malaysia, were reported to be wild-caught (Bezuijen et al. 2012). Ongoing, low-level and opportunistic capture and sale of T. schlegelii by local fishermen occurs in Sarawak.

Wild T. schlegelii are frequently observed along rivers in Kalimantan and Sumatra (e.g. Ross et al. 1998; Bezuijen et al. 2002a, 2002b, 2004; Simpson and Mediyansyah 2009), and are held by local residents as items of curiosity. These individuals are collected on an opportunistic basis and/or are found trapped in fishing nets or traps.
documentation.rationale:
False Gharial (Tomistoma schlegelii) occurs in lowland regions of eastern Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sarawak and Peninsular Malaysia (Malaysia). Severe loss of its swamp forest habitat has occurred over the past three decades at most documented T. schlegelii localities, due to forest fire, logging, plantations, development and/or drainage. Although the species no longer appears to be hunted, eggs and young are collected opportunistically by some local communities, and adults sometimes drown in fishing nets and traps. Other regional threats include opportunistic captures of T. schlegelii for sale to private collections and accidental mortality during river dredging activities.

In the previous assessment in 2011, T. schlegelii was downgraded from Endangered to Vulnerable because surveys indicated the species persisted over a wider global range than previously realised. However, continued survey work since 2011, reaffirms that there are likely to be fewer than 2,500 mature individuals occurring across its range. Declining habitat suitability and continued population declines have also seen a reduction in the number of mature individuals in each subpopulation (fewer than 250 mature individuals in each). This requalifies T. schlegelii as Endangered under criterion C2a(i).

An estimated past reduction of at least 30% is still applicable and although the causes of the population decline are understood, a decline in habitat area and quality are continuing, and the population reduction therefore may not be reversible. Therefore, T. schlegelii qualifies for Vulnerable under criterion A2cd (but must be listed in the higher category of Endangered under criterion C).

The extent of occurrence (EOO) for T. schlegelii is larger than the 20,000 km² threshold for Vulnerable, so criterion B1 does not apply for this species. However, its area of occupancy (AOO) is 684 km², which meets the Vulnerable threshold for criterion of B2. There are approximately 20 subpopulations based on the number of major freshwater river systems inhabited across their range and, with the limited data available, it would appear that individuals remain within a home range and admixture is unlikely; therefore, the population is considered to be severely fragmented (VU B2a). There are also continuing declines in extent of occurrence (EOO); AOO; area, extent and/or quality of habitat; number of locations or subpopulations; and number of mature individuals (VU B2b(i,ii,iii,iv,v)). Again, the species must be listed in the higher category of Endangered under criterion C.

Criterion D does not apply as there are more than 1,000 mature T. schlegelii. No quantitative analysis is available so criterion E cannot be applied.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: The evolutionary relationship of Tomistoma with other crocodilians was debated for many years, and the species was usually aligned with the true crocodiles (Crocodylidae) based on morphological evidence (Norell 1989, Tarsitano et al. 1989, Brochu 1997). Molecular studies since the 1980s suggest a closer relationship to Gavialis (Densmore 1983, Densmore and Dessauer 1984, Gatesy and Amato 1992, Harshman et al. 2003, McAliley et al. 2006). A recent molecular study found that Tomistoma shares gene sequences with Gavialis which are absent from Crocodylus, Mecistops (see Shirley 2010) and Osteolaemus, suggesting Tomistoma should be placed within the family Gavialidae (Willis et al. 2007).
